screens.title: Objectives: Verification & Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: Verification and troubleshooting are as important as configuration. You will learn to use pcs status and corosync-cmapctl to confirm which nodes are members of the ring and whether quorum is present. The chapter gives you a short checklist to diagnose communication failure: firewall rules for UDP 5404 and 5405, network connectivity and correct bindnetaddr, identical corosync. conf files across nodes, and a quick SELinux permissive test. Each checklist item has a concrete action: open the ports using firewall-cmd, ping the bindnetaddr from each node, copy the corosync. conf so the cluster_name and bindnetaddr match, and setenforce 0 to determine if SELinux is blocking traffic. A common misconception is to assume misbehaving nodes will auto-correct their configuration — they will not. Deliberate, identical configuration plus time synchronization fixes most membership issues. This objective ensures you can read the cluster's health output, run a targeted diagnosis, and apply a fix that restores membership. Think about how these checks reduce downtime: quick verification leads to faster remediation and a more reliable HA environment.

Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › Verification & Troubleshooting

Verification & Troubleshooting

Concrete checks to confirm membership and quickly diagnose problems.

Verification commands
sudo pcs status
sudo pcs status corosync
sudo corosync-cmapctl

These commands reveal node membership, resource state, and Corosync cmap values for debugging.

Troubleshooting checklist
  • Open UDP ports 5404 and 5405 on all nodes.
  • Verify ping to the bindnetaddr and correct subnet masks.
  • Ensure /etc/corosync/corosync.conf is identical on all nodes.
  • Temporarily try setenforce 0 to check SELinux interference.
Key Takeaway

A short, repeatable checklist quickly resolves most Corosync membership failures and prevents unnecessary downtime.

Common Mistake

Assuming Corosync will ignore small config mismatches; in practice, even a single differing setting can prevent nodes from joining.

screens.title: What Corosync Does
screens.narratorSegment: Corosync is the distributed messaging and membership layer that allows nodes in a Red Hat HA cluster to communicate reliably and agree on who is part of the cluster. It handles three fundamental responsibilities: message transport between nodes, membership tracking that records which nodes are online, and quorum enforcement to prevent split-brain. A clear example is when a node fails: Corosync removes it from membership and, together with quorum rules, determines whether remaining nodes can continue managing resources. A common misconception is treating Corosync as a resource manager; it is not. Corosync provides the communication fabric and membership decisions while Pacemaker manages resources based on Corosync's information. In practice, you should run Corosync on a dedicated network interface where possible to isolate cluster messages from application traffic and reduce packet loss. Another important operational detail is time synchronization: NTP must be configured on all nodes because time skew can change how messages and timeouts are interpreted, affecting membership decisions. As a takeaway, think of Corosync as the cluster's nervous system — it senses which nodes are alive, sends and receives heartbeat messages, and informs the brain, Pacemaker, so the cluster can act safely. Why would you prefer a dedicated interface and accurate NTP for Corosync traffic?

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › What Corosync Does
Definition

Corosync: messaging, membership, quorum

Corosync provides the cluster with heartbeat messages, membership lists, and quorum voting logic so Pacemaker can manage resources safely.

Message transport: reliable delivery of cluster messages
Membership: who is currently online and part of the ring
Quorum: majority rules to prevent split-brain
Concrete example

If node2 stops responding, Corosync detects the missing heartbeats, updates membership, and combined with quorum settings determines whether node1 alone may continue providing services. In a two-node cluster, two_node: 1 can allow the single remaining node to form quorum; in larger clusters, majority quorum prevents a lone node from running resources.

Misconception

Corosync is not a resource manager. It does not start or stop resources; Pacemaker does that based on Corosync's membership and messaging information.

Key Takeaway

Treat Corosync as the cluster's communication layer and ensure network and time are stable for reliable membership decisions.

screens.title: Install packages and prepare nodes
screens.narratorSegment: The installation and preparation sequence is the first practical step. Install corosync, pacemaker, and pcs on each node so you have both the runtime and the management utility. The canonical command shown in the chapter is sudo dnf install -y corosync pacemaker pcs. After package installation, enable and start the pcsd daemon because pcs commands rely on it; the chapter explicitly instructs enabling pcsd before performing authentication and cluster setup. You must also set a hacluster password on every node so pcs authentication can use it; the hands-on activity uses a password piped into the passwd utility. Configure static IPs for each VM and ensure NTP is running to synchronize clocks. A common mistake is skipping enabling pcsd or forgetting to set the hacluster password on both nodes, which prevents pcs host auth from succeeding. As a concrete scenario, imagine Node1 and Node2 installed packages but Node2 never started pcsd — authentication will fail and cluster setup cannot proceed. The takeaway is that installation is more than a single command: enable necessary daemons, establish a known hacluster credential, and verify time and network settings before attempting to create the cluster. What step would you check first if pcs host auth fails?

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › Install packages and prepare nodes
Procedure

Install and prepare each VM for clustering

Command
sudo dnf install -y corosync pacemaker pcs

Install the runtime and management utilities used to create and manage the cluster.

Enable required services
sudo systemctl enable pcsd
sudo systemctl start pcsd
sudo systemctl status pcsd

pcsd must be running for pcs host authentication and cluster creation to succeed.

Set hacluster password

Use the same password on both nodes so pcs host auth can authenticate between them.

Static IPs

Assign static addresses like 192.168.1.10 and 192.168.1.11 to avoid membership issues caused by address changes.

NTP

Synchronize clocks on all nodes because time skew affects message timeouts and membership decisions.

Key Takeaway

Installation is a short command plus essential follow-up: enable pcsd, set hacluster, confirm network and time sync before cluster creation.

Common Mistake

Skipping pcsd enablement or forgetting the hacluster password on one node will block authentication and setup.

screens.title: corosync.conf structure
screens.narratorSegment: The corosync. conf file controls how Corosync communicates and manages quorum. The chapter provides a simplified example containing totem, quorum, and logging sections. The totem block includes version, cluster_name, secauth, crypto settings, and an interface subsection that specifies ring_number, bindnetaddr, mcastport, and ttl. bindnetaddr is the network address Corosync listens on; for example 192.168.1.0 targets that subnet. The quorum block sets the provider and contains two_node: 1 for two-node clusters — this allows a lone remaining node to form quorum, but only use it in two-node topologies. Logging controls where Corosync writes messages and whether timestamps are enabled. Reviewing the code helps you see why the file must be identical across nodes: differing cluster_name or bindnetaddr means nodes will not join the same ring. Below is the simplified snippet from the chapter; use it as a template and ensure you replace cluster_name and bindnetaddr to match your network. A common misconception is editing only one node and expecting the ring to form — always replicate the same file to all nodes. What would happen if bindnetaddr pointed to the wrong subnet?

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › corosync.conf structure
Configuration example

Use this simplified snippet as a starting template. Ensure identical settings across nodes.

# /etc/corosync/corosync.conf (simplified example)
totem {
    version: 2
    cluster_name: myhacluster
    secauth: on
    crypto_cipher: aes256
    crypto_hash: sha256
    interface {
        ring_number: 0
        bindnetaddr: 192.168.1.0 # Network address for the interface
        mcastport: 5405
        ttl: 1
    }
}

quorum {
    provider: corosync_votequorum
    two_node: 1
}

logging {
    fileline: off
    to_stderr: no
    to_syslog: yes
    syslog_facility: daemon
    debug: off
    timestamp: on
}
Totem

Defines the communication protocol, security options, and which interface or network Corosync uses.

Quorum

Controls vote-based quorum. two_node: 1 is for two-node clusters only; do not enable it for 3+ nodes.

Key Takeaway

Edit corosync.conf carefully, copy the same file to every node, and confirm bindnetaddr and cluster_name match across the cluster.

screens.title: bindnetaddr and network considerations
screens.narratorSegment: bindnetaddr is the network address or interface Corosync uses for inter-node communication. In the provided example bindnetaddr: 192.168.1.0 targets a subnet; Corosync uses that address to bind its sockets. The practical consequence is that bindnetaddr must match the network interface both nodes share for cluster traffic. A common operational pitfall is pointing bindnetaddr to the wrong subnet, which prevents nodes from discovering each other even if IPs and routing look correct. Another best practice from the chapter is to use a dedicated network interface for Corosync traffic to isolate heartbeat and membership messages from application traffic; this reduces contention and packet loss. Remember to open UDP ports 5404 and 5405 for the chosen interface, and verify that network masks and routes allow direct communication between the specified addresses. A concrete example: if Node1 uses 192.168.1.10 and Node2 uses 192.168.1.11, set bindnetaddr to 192.168.1.0 so both IPs fall into the same bind network. Misconfiguring bindnetaddr creates a silent failure where nodes cannot join the same ring despite appearing reachable on other interfaces. The closing question to check your understanding: if nodes can ping each other on their management network but Corosync refuses to form a ring, what network value would you inspect first?

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › bindnetaddr and network considerations
Network detail

bindnetaddr defines the Corosync bind network

What it is

An address representing the network Corosync uses to bind sockets and send cluster messages.

Practical example

Nodes with 192.168.1.10 and 192.168.1.11 should use bindnetaddr: 192.168.1.0 so both addresses are on the same Corosync ring network.

Pitfall

Using the wrong subnet or an interface that is not shared by all nodes causes an inability to form a ring even if other networks are reachable.

Key Takeaway

Confirm the bindnetaddr and that UDP 5404/5405 are open on the interface you chose; mismatches are a top cause of Corosync failures.

screens.title: Quorum and the two_node option
screens.narratorSegment: Quorum is the voting mechanism that prevents split-brain by requiring a majority of nodes to be online before the cluster manages resources. By default, a cluster needs more than half of the votes to form quorum. For a two-node cluster that would mean both nodes must be up, which is often impractical. The chapter explains two_node: 1 as an explicit override that allows a single node in a two-node cluster to form quorum if the other fails. Use this only for two-node topologies; enabling two_node in a three-node cluster is a misconfiguration that undermines majority-based safety and can create split-brain if two nodes fail and the remaining one thinks it has quorum. A concrete scenario: in a two-node lab, setting two_node: 1 lets Node1 continue providing services when Node2 fails, reducing downtime. A misconception is to believe two_node: 1 increases safety in all clusters — it does not. The correct practice for 3+ nodes is to rely on majority quorum (omit two_node or set it to 0) so that a single remaining node cannot operate alone. As a final reflection, consider the trade-off between availability and safety: two_node increases availability for two-member clusters but reduces the strictness of majority consensus that prevents split-brain.

Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › Quorum and the two_node option
Concept

Quorum enforces majority consensus

Majority quorum

By default, the cluster needs more than half of votes to form quorum, preventing a single node from acting alone and creating split-brain.

two_node: 1

In a two-node cluster, set two_node: 1 to allow a single node to form quorum if its peer fails. Do not use this in clusters of 3+ nodes.

Scenario

Two-node lab: with two_node: 1, Node1 continues serving when Node2 goes down — this improves availability but reduces majority strictness.

Key Takeaway

Use two_node only for true two-node clusters; for 3+ nodes rely on majority quorum to preserve safety and avoid split-brain.

screens.title: Troubleshooting checklist
screens.narratorSegment: When nodes do not join the ring or membership is inconsistent, the chapter recommends a focused troubleshooting checklist. First, check the firewall: ensure UDP ports 5404 and 5405 are open on every node so Corosync traffic can pass. Second, verify network connectivity and that each node can ping the bindnetaddr and other nodes on the Corosync network; incorrect subnets or routes are frequent causes. Third, confirm corosync. conf is identical across all nodes; even a small mismatch in cluster_name or bindnetaddr prevents nodes from joining the same cluster. Fourth, consider SELinux: while less commonly the cause, temporarily setting setenforce 0 can reveal whether SELinux policies are blocking Corosync; implement proper policy rather than leaving permissive in production. A concrete troubleshooting sequence is to run firewall-cmd checks, ping tests, a file checksum on corosync. conf across nodes, and then check corosync logs for errors. A frequent misconception is to restart services repeatedly without checking config consistency; restarts will not fix mismatched configuration. screens.title: Operational recommendations
screens.narratorSegment: The chapter emphasizes operational best practices to keep Corosync stable. First, isolate cluster traffic on a dedicated interface where possible; this lowers latency and contention and makes firewall rules clearer. Second, maintain synchronized time across all nodes with NTP because time skew affects message timeouts and membership decisions. Third, replicate corosync. conf to every node and treat it as a versioned artifact under your configuration management workflow so accidental drifts are detected quickly. Fourth, document whether the cluster is two-node or multi-node and set the quorum two_node option only for genuine two-node deployments. Finally, integrate corosync service management into your orchestration: enable corosync at boot and include service health checks in your monitoring systems. A common misconception is that Corosync will automatically select the best interface; it will not — explicit bindnetaddr selection is required. As a closing reflection, consider how small operational choices, like using a dedicated network and version controlling corosync. conf, can prevent most outages and simplify incident diagnosis. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we set up Corosync, the distributed messaging layer that underpins a Red Hat HA cluster. You will learn what Corosync does, why time synchronization and network isolation matter, and the exact configuration pieces in corosync. conf that determine communication, quorum, and logging. We will walk through installing packages, the important directives inside the totem and quorum sections, and the minimal verification steps to confirm cluster membership. As you work, pay attention to the role of bindnetaddr and the special two_node option for two-node clusters — these settings change how quorum is calculated and directly affect whether a remaining node can keep services running after a failure. A concrete example you will see later is a two-node lab using static IPs, pcs authentication, and the pcs cluster setup command, which demonstrates both installation and verification. A common misconception is that Corosync will discover nodes automatically without identical configuration; in reality corosync. conf must match across nodes. By the end of this chapter, you will be able to install corosync and pacemaker, author a consistent corosync. conf, start the service, and verify membership so Pacemaker can safely manage resources. Consider how careful network planning reduces split-brain risk as you begin the lab.

By the end of this chapter you will install and configure Corosync on Red Hat Enterprise Linux, understand the key corosync. conf parameters, create a multi-node cluster that achieves membership and quorum, and verify and troubleshoot Corosync issues. First, you will practice installing the corosync, pacemaker, and pcs packages and enabling the necessary daemons. Next, you will learn to author a consistent /etc/corosync/corosync. conf and inspect the totem, interface, quorum, and logging sections so nodes can communicate reliably. You will also set up a two-node lab that demonstrates the two_node option and why it must be applied only to two-node topologies. Finally, you will run verification commands and perform a small troubleshooting checklist covering firewall, network, configuration consistency, and SELinux checks. Each objective is aimed at giving you hands-on competency: installing packages, preparing network and time sync, producing an identical configuration across nodes, and validating the running cluster. A practical milestone will show you a successful pcs status output listing both nodes. Keep an eye out for the common misconception that Corosync can auto-correct mismatched configs — it cannot; identical configuration is required.

Verification and troubleshooting are as important as configuration. You will learn to use pcs status and corosync-cmapctl to confirm which nodes are members of the ring and whether quorum is present. The chapter gives you a short checklist to diagnose communication failure: firewall rules for UDP 5404 and 5405, network connectivity and correct bindnetaddr, identical corosync. conf files across nodes, and a quick SELinux permissive test. Each checklist item has a concrete action: open the ports using firewall-cmd, ping the bindnetaddr from each node, copy the corosync. conf so the cluster_name and bindnetaddr match, and setenforce 0 to determine if SELinux is blocking traffic. A common misconception is to assume misbehaving nodes will auto-correct their configuration — they will not. Deliberate, identical configuration plus time synchronization fixes most membership issues. This objective ensures you can read the cluster's health output, run a targeted diagnosis, and apply a fix that restores membership. Think about how these checks reduce downtime: quick verification leads to faster remediation and a more reliable HA environment.

Corosync is the distributed messaging and membership layer that allows nodes in a Red Hat HA cluster to communicate reliably and agree on who is part of the cluster. It handles three fundamental responsibilities: message transport between nodes, membership tracking that records which nodes are online, and quorum enforcement to prevent split-brain. A clear example is when a node fails: Corosync removes it from membership and, together with quorum rules, determines whether remaining nodes can continue managing resources. A common misconception is treating Corosync as a resource manager; it is not. Corosync provides the communication fabric and membership decisions while Pacemaker manages resources based on Corosync's information. In practice, you should run Corosync on a dedicated network interface where possible to isolate cluster messages from application traffic and reduce packet loss. Another important operational detail is time synchronization: NTP must be configured on all nodes because time skew can change how messages and timeouts are interpreted, affecting membership decisions. As a takeaway, think of Corosync as the cluster's nervous system — it senses which nodes are alive, sends and receives heartbeat messages, and informs the brain, Pacemaker, so the cluster can act safely. Why would you prefer a dedicated interface and accurate NTP for Corosync traffic?

The installation and preparation sequence is the first practical step. Install corosync, pacemaker, and pcs on each node so you have both the runtime and the management utility. The canonical command shown in the chapter is sudo dnf install -y corosync pacemaker pcs. After package installation, enable and start the pcsd daemon because pcs commands rely on it; the chapter explicitly instructs enabling pcsd before performing authentication and cluster setup. You must also set a hacluster password on every node so pcs authentication can use it; the hands-on activity uses a password piped into the passwd utility. Configure static IPs for each VM and ensure NTP is running to synchronize clocks. A common mistake is skipping enabling pcsd or forgetting to set the hacluster password on both nodes, which prevents pcs host auth from succeeding. As a concrete scenario, imagine Node1 and Node2 installed packages but Node2 never started pcsd — authentication will fail and cluster setup cannot proceed. The takeaway is that installation is more than a single command: enable necessary daemons, establish a known hacluster credential, and verify time and network settings before attempting to create the cluster. What step would you check first if pcs host auth fails?

The corosync. conf file controls how Corosync communicates and manages quorum. The chapter provides a simplified example containing totem, quorum, and logging sections. The totem block includes version, cluster_name, secauth, crypto settings, and an interface subsection that specifies ring_number, bindnetaddr, mcastport, and ttl. bindnetaddr is the network address Corosync listens on; for example 192.168.1.0 targets that subnet. The quorum block sets the provider and contains two_node: 1 for two-node clusters — this allows a lone remaining node to form quorum, but only use it in two-node topologies. Logging controls where Corosync writes messages and whether timestamps are enabled. Reviewing the code helps you see why the file must be identical across nodes: differing cluster_name or bindnetaddr means nodes will not join the same ring. Below is the simplified snippet from the chapter; use it as a template and ensure you replace cluster_name and bindnetaddr to match your network. A common misconception is editing only one node and expecting the ring to form — always replicate the same file to all nodes. What would happen if bindnetaddr pointed to the wrong subnet?

bindnetaddr is the network address or interface Corosync uses for inter-node communication. In the provided example bindnetaddr: 192.168.1.0 targets a subnet; Corosync uses that address to bind its sockets. The practical consequence is that bindnetaddr must match the network interface both nodes share for cluster traffic. A common operational pitfall is pointing bindnetaddr to the wrong subnet, which prevents nodes from discovering each other even if IPs and routing look correct. Another best practice from the chapter is to use a dedicated network interface for Corosync traffic to isolate heartbeat and membership messages from application traffic; this reduces contention and packet loss. Remember to open UDP ports 5404 and 5405 for the chosen interface, and verify that network masks and routes allow direct communication between the specified addresses. A concrete example: if Node1 uses 192.168.1.10 and Node2 uses 192.168.1.11, set bindnetaddr to 192.168.1.0 so both IPs fall into the same bind network. Misconfiguring bindnetaddr creates a silent failure where nodes cannot join the same ring despite appearing reachable on other interfaces. The closing question to check your understanding: if nodes can ping each other on their management network but Corosync refuses to form a ring, what network value would you inspect first?

Quorum is the voting mechanism that prevents split-brain by requiring a majority of nodes to be online before the cluster manages resources. By default, a cluster needs more than half of the votes to form quorum. For a two-node cluster that would mean both nodes must be up, which is often impractical. The chapter explains two_node: 1 as an explicit override that allows a single node in a two-node cluster to form quorum if the other fails. Use this only for two-node topologies; enabling two_node in a three-node cluster is a misconfiguration that undermines majority-based safety and can create split-brain if two nodes fail and the remaining one thinks it has quorum. A concrete scenario: in a two-node lab, setting two_node: 1 lets Node1 continue providing services when Node2 fails, reducing downtime. A misconception is to believe two_node: 1 increases safety in all clusters — it does not. The correct practice for 3+ nodes is to rely on majority quorum (omit two_node or set it to 0) so that a single remaining node cannot operate alone. As a final reflection, consider the trade-off between availability and safety: two_node increases availability for two-member clusters but reduces the strictness of majority consensus that prevents split-brain.

After you have a correct corosync. conf on every node, enable and start the corosync service so nodes begin forming the ring. The chapter lists a minimal sequence: sudo systemctl enable corosync, sudo systemctl start corosync, and sudo systemctl status corosync to check runtime status. You might also start the cluster with pcs cluster start --all after performing pcs cluster setup; the hands-on walkthrough shows creating the cluster with pcs cluster setup myhacluster node1. example. com node2. example. com --force then starting the cluster. Verification steps include pcs status and sudo pcs status corosync to show member nodes. As a concrete example, after copying the same corosync. conf to both VMs and starting corosync, run sudo pcs status; you should see both nodes listed and the ring healthy. When nodes do not join the ring or membership is inconsistent, the chapter recommends a focused troubleshooting checklist. First, check the firewall: ensure UDP ports 5404 and 5405 are open on every node so Corosync traffic can pass. Second, verify network connectivity and that each node can ping the bindnetaddr and other nodes on the Corosync network; incorrect subnets or routes are frequent causes. Third, confirm corosync. conf is identical across all nodes; even a small mismatch in cluster_name or bindnetaddr prevents nodes from joining the same cluster. Fourth, consider SELinux: while less commonly the cause, temporarily setting setenforce 0 can reveal whether SELinux policies are blocking Corosync; implement proper policy rather than leaving permissive in production. A concrete troubleshooting sequence is to run firewall-cmd checks, ping tests, a file checksum on corosync. conf across nodes, and then check corosync logs for errors. A frequent misconception is to restart services repeatedly without checking config consistency; restarts will not fix mismatched configuration. The chapter emphasizes operational best practices to keep Corosync stable. First, isolate cluster traffic on a dedicated interface where possible; this lowers latency and contention and makes firewall rules clearer. Second, maintain synchronized time across all nodes with NTP because time skew affects message timeouts and membership decisions. Third, replicate corosync. conf to every node and treat it as a versioned artifact under your configuration management workflow so accidental drifts are detected quickly. Finally, integrate corosync service management into your orchestration: enable corosync at boot and include service health checks in your monitoring systems.
